action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen
action_criteria.rationale: A MoCA documents his frontal-subcortical deficits, which have already caused missed insulin doses, and gives a baseline to repeat after the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 42 mL removed; TUG 34 to 22 s (35%) at 24 hours
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test: opening pressure, routine CSF and removal of 30-50 mL
action_criteria.rationale: Removing 42 mL with normal opening pressure and normal CSF content tests whether his gait improves when CSF is drained despite his white matter disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 24 s at 2 hours and 22 s at 24 hours (35% faster), 10-m walk 18 s (36% faster), MoCA 23/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating his rollator-assisted TUG and 10-m walk at 2 and 24 hours after the 42 mL tap shows whether his gait responds to CSF removal despite the white matter change.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not withhold shunt referral because of the Fazekas 2 white matter change; patients with iNPH and white matter disease also improve after shunting [Tisell_2011]
Do not attribute the magnetic gait with freezing to diabetic peripheral neuropathy
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 35% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Arrange supervision of insulin and metformin by his wife or granddaughter, since memory impairment has already caused missed insulin doses
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: He has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address his progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
His falls happened on starting to walk or turning without loss of consciousness, so an ECG does not explain them.
He has no cardiac symptoms or embolic events, and an echocardiogram does not inform the iNPH work-up.
An outside CT already showed enlarged ventricles; MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH, white matter and hippocampi better.
There is no syncope or palpitation history, so ambulatory rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
An 18-month course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change in a hypertensive diabetic former smoker may contribute, but ventriculomegaly with DESH and a 35% TUG improvement after the tap are not explained by small-vessel disease.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic sensory polyneuropathy as the cause of the gait disorder
differential.key_features: Mild distal vibration loss fits a neuropathy, but light touch and joint position are intact and a neuropathy does not cause freezing or improve after CSF removal.
Freezing on initiation overlaps, but there is no tremor or rigidity and the wide-based gait improves after the tap.
Gait came first, recall recovers with cueing, MTA is 2 (within the range for age 75) and the MoCA rises after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles disproportionate to cortical volume loss, tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic) communicating hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: There is no history of head injury, haemorrhage or meningitis before the gait decline.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; he has all three over 18 months [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.41 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 68 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 15 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]
After removal of 42 mL, TUG fell from 34 to 22 s (35%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 28 to 18 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive criterion [Nakajima_2021]
Fazekas 2 white matter change coexists with iNPH and does not preclude shunt benefit [Tisell_2011]
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A mild distal neuropathy may add to imbalance, but it does not produce a magnetic gait with freezing, urinary urgency or a gait that improves after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Mildly reduced vibration at both ankles and distal feet
red_herrings.intended_effect: The gait disorder is attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 75-year-old retired city bus driver with hypertension, type 2 diabetes on insulin, and CKD stage 2 was admitted for evaluation of progressive functional decline over the past 18 months. He and his wife first noticed his walking became slower and less coordinated about 18 months ago. He describes difficulty 'getting started walking': once in motion he can walk, but initiating the first steps feels like his feet are 'glued to the floor.' He has had five falls while starting to walk or turning, without loss of consciousness, including one that caused a right wrist sprain. He now uses a four-wheeled rollator walker and requires his wife's assistance for outdoor walks. Urinary urgency and incontinence developed approximately 12 months ago with daily near-accidents and at least four actual incontinence episodes per week. His wife handles his protective underwear. Cognitive changes have been progressive: he forgets grocery lists, cannot recall recent conversations, and has missed insulin doses several times because he forgot whether he had taken it. He has always been a disciplined, schedule-oriented person from his driving career. His granddaughter, who has a nursing background, pushed for neurological evaluation. A head CT obtained three months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. His primary care physician referred him for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary incontinence.

neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Snout reflex. No nuchal rigidity.

neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, severely apraxic shuffling gait. Prominent freezing on initiation. Very short steps, en-bloc turning; walks with a rollator. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test: 3 steps backward.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place; uncertain of date. Slowed responses, no aphasia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength throughout. No resting tremor. No rigidity.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mildly reduced vibration at both ankles and distal feet. Light touch and joint position intact.
